question: A product team needs to compare yearly revenue by city and product category across several operational systems. Which design best matches the workload?
options: Create an integrated historical warehouse with a sales fact and consistent product, location and time dimensions
Build a replicated OLTP order database and run each yearly report through transactional point lookups
Use a search index over raw order documents, then infer city and category totals independently in each source
Expose each source as an isolated data mart without common customer or product identifiers across systems
explanation: A warehouse integrates sources and supports historical, aggregate OLAP queries. OLTP is optimized for short operational transactions rather than broad multidimensional analysis.
source: L7 slides 14-20 (OLTP versus OLAP, warehouse characteristics and architecture); Elmasri/Navathe, Overview of Data Warehousing and OLAP, ch. 29.

question: SalesFact stores one row per sold product line. A shipment table stores three shipment rows for an order with two sales lines. Why could joining both tables on order_id and then summing sales revenue be wrong?
options: A fact-to-fact join preserves revenue sums because both tables reference the same order identifier
Aggregating by order after the join removes shipment duplication, because order IDs define a unique fact grain
Each sales-line amount can appear once per matching shipment, inflating the revenue sum across joined rows
A sales fact cannot be joined to shipments unless the two tables have identical columns and physical row counts
explanation: The join can produce 2 × 3 = 6 rows for that order; each original sale line may be counted three times. Aggregation should respect the facts’ grains, not assume a join preserves measures.
source: L7 slides 59-64 and 91-92 (fact schemas, fact constellations and warehouse design).

question: A product dimension contains product, brand and supplier details. Which structural change most clearly makes a star design more snowflake-like?
options: Put all brand, supplier and product properties inside SalesFact to reduce the number of dimension references
Move brand or supplier hierarchies into linked dimension tables, normalizing the original product dimension
Add a separate daily sales fact with the same product dimension, turning the original star into a normalized snowflake
Duplicate the product attributes for every sale line, making the product table unnecessary for joins
explanation: Snowflake designs normalize dimension hierarchies into separate tables, reducing redundancy but creating additional joins. Moving measures into dimensions does not define a snowflake.
source: L7 slides 59-63 (star, snowflake and constellation examples); Elmasri/Navathe, Overview of Data Warehousing and OLAP, ch. 29.

question: A data cube has exactly three independent dimensions and no additional hierarchy levels. How many distinct GROUP BY subsets (cuboids) does its full CUBE contain, including the apex and base?
explanation: Each dimension is either included or aggregated away, giving 2^3 = 8 subsets. Three dimensions does not imply only three cuboids; the empty subset is the grand-total apex.
source: L7 slides 74-82 (multidimensional data and cuboid lattice).

question: A report changes from sales by (product, country, month) to sales by (product, country, year). Which OLAP operation occurred?
options: Roll-up: replace the month level with its coarser year level along the time hierarchy
Pivot: swap the displayed time dimension with product, retaining the same grouping granularity
Slice: choose one fixed time value and remove the other periods from the report result
Drill-down: move to a finer-grained time level by replacing years with their months
explanation: Month → year moves upward in the time hierarchy, reducing detail: roll-up. Drill-down goes in the opposite direction; pivot only reorients displayed axes.
source: L7 slides 71-72 and 84-87 (hierarchies, roll-up and drill-down).

question: An analyst fixes city = Oslo and then restricts month to January or February and product to A or B. Which descriptions apply?
options: A drill-down on city followed by a roll-up over selected months, reducing both dimension detail and filter scope
A slice fixing the city and a dice restricting selected values of month and product
A roll-up from city to country followed by a slice that removes the time dimension
A pivot moving city to columns and a drill-down that adds additional hierarchy levels
explanation: Slice selects one dimension value; dice selects a subcube over ranges/sets in multiple dimensions. Neither is the same as reorienting axes (pivot).
source: L7 slides 84-89 (OLAP slice, dice, roll-up, drill-down and pivot).

question: According to Chai et al., which sequence most accurately allocates work across the ML data-management lifecycle?
options: Pre-ML focuses on model serving, in-ML reconciles source schemas, and post-ML handles input labeling and cleaning
Pre-ML prepares and labels data, in-ML supports features and training, and post-ML versions, serves and debugs models
Pre-ML performs the training, in-ML validates a fixed model, and post-ML extracts features from operational databases
Pre-ML builds model registries, in-ML audits source permissions, and post-ML prepares and labels input data
explanation: The survey distinguishes preparing high-quality data, accelerating training/inference, and managing deployed models and pipelines. It explicitly treats post-training data/artifact management as part of the problem.
source: L7 slides 4-8; Chai et al. (2023), Data Management for Machine Learning: A Survey, §§1-4.

question: In five baskets, X appears in four baskets, Y in three, and both X and Y in two. What are the support and confidence of X ⇒ Y?
options: Support 2/4; confidence 2/5
Support 3/5; confidence 2/3
Support 4/5; confidence 3/5
Support 2/5; confidence 2/4
explanation: Support counts baskets containing both items divided by all baskets: 2/5 = 0.4. Confidence conditions on X appearing: 2/4 = 0.5. These measure co-occurrence, not causation.
source: Elmasri/Navathe, Data Mining Concepts, §28.2.1, printed pp. 1073-1075; Garcia-Molina/Ullman/Widom, Data Mining §20.6.

question: When Apriori discovers that itemset {A,B} is below the minimum support threshold, what can it safely infer?
options: Every superset containing {A,B} is also infrequent, since adding items cannot increase support in the data
Every subset of {A,B} is infrequent, since removing a condition cannot increase the matching basket count
Every rule with antecedent A has confidence below the threshold, since {A,B} failed minimum support
Every other two-item combination is infrequent, since one infrequent pair excludes the remaining candidates
explanation: Support is anti-monotone under addition of items: a superset cannot occur in more baskets than {A,B}. Pruning supersets is safe, while its subsets can still be frequent.
source: Elmasri/Navathe, Data Mining Concepts, §28.2.2 (Apriori), printed pp. 1075-1076.
